summary: This memo defines managed objects corresponding to the parties, contexts, and access control policies of the SNMPv2 administrative model. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This paper lists the things you can look up about who is allowed to manage a device. It is historic.

questions: what is an access control list in snmp
subtitle: Managed objects defining parties, authentication, privacy, and access control for SNMPv2.

tldr.problem: SNMPv2 adds security to network management through authentication and encryption, but these capabilities need to be managed through standard objects that describe who can do what.
tldr.mechanism: The Party MIB defines tables and objects for managing parties (agents and managers), contexts (administrative domains), access control policies, and MIB views that define what data each party can access.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1447 is marked Historic; SNMPv3 replaced SNMPv2's party-based security model with a simpler user-based model that became the standard for SNMP security.

today: RFC 1447 is marked Historic. SNMPv3 (introduced in RFC 3414) replaced the party-based security model with a simpler User-Based Security Model (USM) that focuses on users rather than parties, and added role-based access control. Modern SNMP deployments use SNMPv3, which is more straightforward and is the current standard.

sections.title: SNMPv2 Security Through Parties
sections.content:
SNMPv2 builds security into network management by introducing parties, which represent either agents (devices being managed) or managers (management stations). Each party has an authentication protocol (such as MD5) to prove its identity and a privacy protocol (such as DES) to encrypt messages. A party can also have a password or secret key needed for authentication.

The Party MIB standardizes how these security parameters are managed. A manager needs to be able to query and configure which parties exist, what authentication and encryption they use, and what access rights they have. This RFC defines managed objects that allow a management station to view and configure all of these settings through standard SNMP operations.
sections.eli5: When you want to securely manage a device, you create an identity (a party) with a password and decide whether to encrypt the traffic. This document describes how to store and manage those identities.

sections.title: Key Concepts: Parties, Contexts, and Views
sections.content:
A party is a unique identity in SNMPv2, identified by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER. Each party has authentication credentials (a public value and a private key for MD5, or no credentials for unauthenticated access) and privacy settings (DES encryption or no encryption). A party can be local (running on this SNMPv2 entity) or remote (running on another system). A party also has a transport address (typically an IP address and UDP port).

A context represents an administrative scope or domain. It can be a local MIB view (a set of objects this agent maintains) or a proxy relationship pointing to another agent's context. Contexts allow an SNMPv2 entity to manage multiple distinct information spaces.

An access control policy defines what operations a subject party (a manager) can perform on a target party (an agent) when accessing a particular context. For example, a read-only manager might be allowed only Get and GetNext operations on system information. A write-capable manager might be allowed Get, GetNext, and Set operations on configuration objects.

A MIB view further restricts what objects a party can access by specifying which branches of the MIB tree are included or excluded. A view can use wildcards to include or exclude families of related objects.
sections.eli5: A party is a user with a name and password. A context is a group of objects (like system info or network settings). Access control says which user can do what in which group. Views are like permission filters that say 'you can see this part of the data but not that part.'

sections.title: Party Database Objects
sections.content:
The partyTable is the core MIB structure. Each row represents one party with the following managed objects:

  • partyIdentity: the unique identifier (object ID) for the party.
  • partyAuthProtocol: either noAuth (no authentication) or v2md5AuthProtocol (MD5 authentication).
  • partyAuthPrivate: the private authentication key (MD5 secret). For security, this value is write-only and always returns zero when read.
  • partyAuthClock: a counter to prevent replay attacks. The clock is incremented by the authentication protocol and must only decrease if the private key is changed.
  • partyAuthLifetime: the maximum acceptable delay for messages from this party (in seconds), protecting against very old replayed messages.
  • partyPrivProtocol: either noPriv (no encryption) or desPrivProtocol (DES encryption).
  • partyPrivPrivate: the private encryption key (DES secret), also write-only.
  • partyTDomain and partyTAddress: the transport protocol and address where the party receives traffic.

Initial parties are assigned standard object identifiers so that devices can be configured with default read-only and read-write parties without prior coordination.
sections.eli5: The party table lists all the identities on a device, with their passwords, security settings, and where they listen for messages. The passwords are secret and can't be read back, only changed.

sections.title: Contexts and Access Control
sections.content:
The contextTable defines SNMPv2 contexts. A context can be a local context (a subtree of objects on the local agent) or a proxy context (a reference to objects on another agent). For local contexts, the table includes a contextViewIndex that identifies which MIB view applies. For proxy contexts, it includes destination party and source party information specifying how to reach the remote agent.

The aclTable (access control list table) defines access policies. Each row specifies a combination of aclTarget (the agent being managed), aclSubject (the manager making the request), and aclResources (the context being accessed). The aclPrivileges field is a bitmask of allowed operations: Get (1), GetNext (2), Response (4), Set (8), GetBulk (32), Inform (64), and SNMPv2-Trap (128).

The viewTable defines MIB views by specifying subtrees that are included or excluded. A viewSubtree is an object identifier (like 1.3.6.1.2.1 for system objects), and viewMask is a bitmask allowing wildcards. Multiple entries in the view table can be combined to create complex access policies.
sections.eli5: Contexts say 'this is a group of data to manage.' Access control rules say 'this manager can do these operations in this context.' Views say 'you can see this part of the tree but not that part.'

sections.title: Initial Configuration and Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC defines standard initial parties and contexts that all SNMPv2 agents should support. For an agent at IP address a.b.c.d, initial party identifiers include noAuth/noPriv parties for both agent and manager roles, and md5Auth/desPriv parties for both roles. This allows basic SNMPv2 communication to be bootstrapped without prior configuration of secrets.

The RFC specifies three supported security combinations: noAuth/noPriv (no authentication or encryption, simplest), md5Auth/noPriv (authenticated but unencrypted), and md5Auth/desPriv (both authenticated and encrypted, most secure). The authentication clock mechanism prevents replay attacks by requiring that subsequent messages from a party have a higher clock value.

Key changes are handled carefully: the partyAuthPrivate and partyPrivPrivate fields use XOR encoding for updates, allowing a manager to change a secret key without being able to read the old key. The partyCloneFrom field allows creating new parties by cloning security parameters from existing parties, simplifying bulk configuration.
sections.eli5: The RFC defines standard settings for new devices: who authenticates with what password, whether messages are encrypted, and how to prevent old messages from being replayed. Secrets are changed using XOR so no one ever reads the old secret.
